Add your API key

Connection

Tap Save to apply

Your key is encrypted at rest and only used to generate your personal exercise sets and reviews. Usage is tracked per-user for transparency.

Paste an Anthropic key (console.anthropic.com, starts with sk-ant-), a Google Gemini key (aistudio.google.com, starts with AQ. or the older AIza), or an OpenAI key (platform.openai.com, starts with sk-proj-).

A key replaces the one saved for its provider and switches to it. Keys for other providers stay saved.

Provider in use

Switch between the keys you've saved. To add another provider, paste its key above.

Ruby / Rails (default)

Choose the language your daily exercise sets are generated in. "Mixed" alternates between Ruby/Rails and JavaScript one full day at a time.

Your day

UTC

Sets when your day rolls over and when your 8am exercise set is generated. Leave on "detect automatically" to use your browser's zone.

Daily sections

Automatic gives you shorter sets after days you don't finish, and longer ones once you finish more and your reviewed answers go well. A number sets how many sections each day is planned with, though a section that fails a quality check can still be left out. 2 gives you only Code Review and Design Comparison.

Junior

The level every section uses unless you set one for it in the Exercise mix below. Your ratings nudge each day's set around it. Changing your track also moves any section set to your old or new level, unless it is locked. When your reviewed answers show a section is ready to move, Coding Gym suggests a level for that section, and you decide. Principal engineer is set only here; Coding Gym never suggests it.

Exercise mix

When this is off, the dashboard stops suggesting level changes. You can still change levels yourself below, and turn this back on at any time.

Bias how often each rotating section appears, and set how hard any section is pitched. Neither changes how many sections a day holds — that's the setting above. Changes save automatically.

Skipping is a stronger, different action than turning a slider down.

A slider at Much less means rarely — the section can still come up, and it will if you haven't seen it in a long while, so nothing disappears from your rotation permanently.

Skip means never. The section is removed from rotation entirely and will not appear again until you turn Skip off.

Skipping also makes the whole group come up less often on shorter days. Fewer kinds left means the ones that remain are seen more often and stay fresh, so the group gives way to groups holding something you haven't seen.

Locking a difficulty target

Lock means this section is always pitched at the level you chose. Easing for concepts you're finding hard, and adjustments from your difficulty ratings, stop applying to it — including the first time you meet a concept. Your progress is still tracked, and unlocking uses it again straight away.

In every set
Code Review
Difficulty target

0 of 44 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Code Review

Find the one problem in a short piece of code and say how you'd fix it. This builds the habit of reading a change closely before you approve it.

Example: You see a ten-line method from a library app that emails members about overdue books. The question asks what's wrong with it and how you'd fix it. On some days the code is a test file or a database migration instead.

Design Comparison
Difficulty target

0 of 20 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Design Comparison

Two pieces of code both work, and you pick the one that suits the system described. Then you name the fact from the scenario or question that decides it.

Example: A grocery list app will add new kinds of items later. Piece A and Piece B both save an item today, built two different ways. You choose one and point to the sentence that settles it.

Pattern section, in some sets
Pattern of the Month
Difficulty target

0 of 44 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Pattern of the Month

This section names a design pattern and why it exists, then asks how you'd apply it to a stated problem. The answer box starts with headings for the parts a full answer covers.

Example: The setting is a gym log, where one button saves a workout, updates a streak and sends a message. You're asked how you'd structure the work using the day's pattern, and you describe it in words.

Rotating third section
Default
Difficulty target

0 of 15 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Architecture Decision

Choose between two or three ways to build something, and justify the choice by what each one costs. You write reasoning, not code.

Example: A library app has to tell members when a book they reserved comes back. One option checks every few minutes, and another reacts the moment the book is returned. You pick one for the situation described and say what you'd give up.

Default
Difficulty target

0 of 2 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Security Review

Find the one weakness someone could exploit in a short piece of code, and say how you'd close it. It trains you to read code the way an attacker would.

Example: You see a short controller action that shows a shared shopping list. The question asks what someone could exploit here and how you'd stop it.

Default
Difficulty target

0 of 44 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Coding Challenge

Write working code for a small task the question describes. Some days you start from a skeleton, and other days from an empty box.

Example: The task is a method that sorts a shopping list by aisle, with a sentence saying what it should return. You write the method in the answer box.

Default
Difficulty target

0 of 20 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Parsons Problem

Put shuffled pieces of code back in the order that works. Drag them into place, or move them with the keyboard.

Example: A short method that totals a gym member's weekly workouts arrives in a random order. You arrange the pieces until the method would run and give the right total.

At least one section in this group has to stay in rotation.

Rotating fourth section
Default
Difficulty target

0 of 4 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Plan Review

Read an implementation plan, written as if by an AI assistant, before any code exists. Say what you'd push back on, since a problem costs less to fix in a plan than in finished code.

Example: The plan lays out five steps for letting gym members export their workout history. You're asked what you'd want changed before you approve it.

Default
Difficulty target

0 of 5 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Ambiguity Hunt

Read a vague feature request and write down what you'd need clarified before you could build it. Asking early costs less than building the wrong thing.

Example: A product manager writes: “Let people pause their daily practice while they're on holiday.” You're asked what you'd need answered before building it.

Default
Difficulty target

0 of 8 concepts have AI difficulty guidance.

About Pseudocode to Code

Write the steps to solve a problem in plain words, without worrying about syntax. When your answer is reviewed, Coding Gym turns your steps into code exactly as written, so you can see what a missing step would do.

Example: The problem is merging overlapping bookings in a meeting room's calendar. You write your steps, and “Check my plan” can point out gaps before you submit.

At least one section in this group has to stay in rotation.

Optional: prepare concept-specific guidance that tells the AI what problems at each section's level should look like. Your levels work without it. The count is the concepts behind your sections' levels that still need guidance; this does not generate a new exercise set.
